enso.headline: A very strong El Niño is building, and it could be one of the strongest on record.
enso.readingNote: above normal in the key Niño-3.4 zone of the Pacific, week of September 23
points: What it's doing now: El Niño has supercharged the eastern Pacific hurricane season. Hurricane Polo reached Category 5 three times, and its remains flooded southern New Mexico on Sept. 29 and 30, pushing McLeod Dam in Doña Ana County close to failure and forcing hundreds of people to evacuate. Hurricane Rachel, the Pacific's 20th named storm this year, is sending more tropical moisture into Texas and the central U.S.

Not every storm is El Niño: the nor'easter that hit New York and Long Island Sept. 23 to 27 grew from an ordinary upper-level low. El Niño's biggest push on East Coast storms usually comes in winter, when it strengthens the southern storm track.
NOAA gives a greater than 90% chance of a very strong El Niño this fall and winter, and a 75% chance it becomes the strongest since records began in 1950.
Forecasters expect it to last through winter and into spring 2027.

For La Porte and the Great Lakes: strong El Niño winters usually run warmer than normal across the northern U.S., and the Ohio Valley tends to be drier. That often means less snow here, but not every time. Weather.com's Oct. 1 winter outlook also expects a mild winter for the Midwest and Great Lakes, and notes that with less snow, more storms may bring rain or freezing rain instead. Keep your winter gear ready.
Around the world, strong El Niños tend to bring heavy rain and flooding to parts of South America and East Africa, and drought to parts of Australia, Indonesia and southern Africa.

climate.headline: The climate is warming. Here's what that means, calmly.

points.fact: 2024 was the warmest year on record so far, and the ten warmest years on record have all come in the last decade.
points.doThis: Heat is the deadliest kind of weather in the U.S. Know the signs of heat illness and check on neighbors during heat waves.

points.fact: A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so heavy downpours are getting heavier, including in the Midwest.
points.doThis: Know if your home or road floods, keep gutters and storm drains clear, and never drive through water over the road.

points.fact: El Niño on top of a warmer baseline makes new global heat records more likely in 2026 and 2027.
points.doThis: Expect more extremes, not just warmer days: have a basic kit ready and more than one way to get warnings.
